# Partition study notebook

## Prior testable expectations

**H1 [tentative].** Target partition depends on the solvent-S / extractant-X pairing rather than either anonymous index alone. Under matched phase volumes and mixing, some pairings should reproducibly shift `product_in_organic` versus `product_in_aqueous`; equal numeric labels have no privileged meaning.

**H2 [tentative].** At fixed material pairing, increasing organic phase fraction should raise the fraction of the fixed initial target inventory found in the organic phase, while an underlying concentration partition tendency may remain approximately stable. I will distinguish inventory fractions from concentrations and compute only volume-aware ratios.

**H3 [tentative].** Mixing controls approach to partition equilibrium: weak/short mixing may produce lower equilibrium confidence or a different split than stronger/longer mixing, but an over-mixing penalty remains an alternative.

**Design decision.** Use all 12 independent batches with one pre-separation HPLC each, varying pairings, phase amounts, and mixing. HPLC is explicitly before `separate_phase`; final assays follow explicit termination. Retention will be varied to confirm that separation removes the nonrequested phase rather than acting as a sampling selector. Numerical differences will not be called effects without repeat or uncertainty support.

# Partition study notebook

## Priors

**H1 [tentative].** Target partition depends on solvent-S / extractant-X pairing; anonymous numeric labels carry no implied relation.

**H2 [tentative].** Increasing organic phase fraction should raise the fraction of the fixed initial target inventory in organic, requiring volume-aware interpretation rather than treating inventory fractions as concentrations.

**H3 [tentative].** Mixing controls approach to partition equilibrium, with over-mixing remaining an alternative.

## Interim commitments

**H1 [supported for one-factor changes around S0/X0; interactions unresolved].** At fixed nominal volumes and mixing, changing X at S0 produced sizable shifts in pre-separation organic inventory: X0 0.152 (event runner-operation-0007), X1 0.315 (0017), X2 0.211 (0027), X3 0.375 (0037). Changing S at X0 also shifted it: S0 exact repeats 0.152 and 0.165 (0007, 0077), versus S1 0.304 (0047), S2 0.229 (0057), S3 0.338 (0067). The S0/X0 repeat difference is small relative to many material contrasts and the declared HPLC noise scale, supporting a real material effect in this local design. However, only a star around S0/X0 was tested, so solvent–extractant interaction and transferability to other pairings remain unresolved.

**H4 [supported operational interpretation].** Pre-separation HPLC observes both phases, whereas phase retention removes the other phase. Organic-retained final assays had phase ratio near 1 and aqueous target near zero (events 0030, 0050, 0070); aqueous-retained assays had phase ratio near 0 and organic target near zero (0020, 0040, 0060, 0080). Small nonzero opposite-phase readings are compatible with sampling/noise and are not evidence that separation is a sampling switch.

## Next predictions (written before phase-volume and mixing tests)

At S0/X0, raising extractant volume while lowering added aqueous volume should increase organic phase ratio and organic inventory; reversing those volumes should decrease both. Weak mixing should leave a split different from the 300 s/600 rpm repeat baseline if mass transfer is incomplete. A longer/faster mix will test whether the baseline is already near a plateau; if it agrees within measurement variation, H3 will be narrowed to weak-mixing conditions.

notes.text:
# Partition study notebook

## Final source-stage commitments

**H1 [supported in the tested local design; pairing interactions unresolved].** Material choice substantially changes partition. At common nominal volumes and 300 s/600 rpm, S0 with X0/X1/X2/X3 gave pre-separation organic inventory fractions 0.152, 0.315, 0.211, 0.375 (events runner-operation-0007, 0017, 0027, 0037). With X0, S0/S1/S2/S3 gave 0.152, 0.304, 0.229, 0.338 (0007, 0047, 0057, 0067). Exact S0/X0 repetition gave 0.165 organic (0077), close to 0.152 relative to most material contrasts. Thus both anonymous material categories matter; the data do not establish additivity or predict untested cross-pairings because only a star design was used.

**H2 [supported for inventory fractions; approximate concentration-ratio invariance only].** At S0/X0 and common mixing, changing added aqueous/extractant from 0.055/0.005 through 0.040/0.020 to 0.020/0.040 moved observed phase ratio from 0.059 (0097), approximately 0.169–0.178 in exact baseline repeats (0007, 0077), to 0.394 (0087), and organic inventory from 0.067 to 0.152–0.165 to 0.355. This is the predicted direction. Volume-aware apparent concentration ratios `K=(Fo/Fa)*(1-r)/r` were about 1.13, 0.93–0.94, and 0.87, respectively. Their spread may reflect HPLC noise amplified at low phase volume, phase-volume response, or genuine nonideality; therefore constant K is only an approximate local description, not a confirmed law. Solvent addition and the initial liquid are part of actual volume, so added aqueous volume alone is not the aqueous volume.

**H3 [unresolved, with scope narrowed].** Weak 10 s/100 rpm mixing gave organic inventory 0.152 (0107), overlapping the 0.152 and 0.165 baseline repeats, so there is no clear evidence that this weak condition is deficient. Long/fast 1200 s/1000 rpm gave 0.225 (0117), a numerical increase larger than the repeat spread. Duration and speed were changed together, there is only one run, and purity/closure also differed; enhanced transfer, process change, and chance/noise remain alternatives. A decisive follow-up would independently vary duration and speed with repeats.

**H4 [supported operational interpretation].** HPLC measurements above occurred before phase removal and reported both phase inventories. After `separate_phase`, organic-retained final assays had phase ratio near 1 and aqueous target near zero, while aqueous-retained assays had phase ratio near 0 and organic target near zero (e.g. 0030/0050/0070/0090/0110 versus 0020/0040/0060/0080/0100/0120). Small opposite-phase values were not interpreted as true zero/nonzero distinctions because sampling and instrument noise affect closure. Separation retains the requested phase and removes the other.

## Limits and testable consequences

The design supports local interpolation for tested S0/X0 phase amounts but not extrapolation to untested material cross-pairs, repeated-stage extraction, other total volumes, or independently controlled mixing variables. Inventory closure `Fo+Fa` varied around unity, so neither missing measurements nor closure deviations were assigned as zero. Future blind predictions should carry wider uncertainty for untested cross-pairings and extreme phase ratios, and phase-retention predictions must be based on whether organic or aqueous target inventory is sought rather than treating retention as a measurement setting.

payload.report:
Observations — Supplied information identified S0–S3 and X0–X3 only as independent anonymous benchmark materials; equal indices imply no shared identity or property, and no property dossier was supplied. Thus the material trends below come from the experiments, not prior chemical knowledge. The instrument contract also established that HPLC could observe both phase inventories before separation, with declared noise scales of about 0.015 for each product channel and 0.018 for phase ratio.

At the common recipe (0.020 mol reagent, 0.040 L solvent, 0.040 L added aqueous phase, 0.020 L extractant, 300 s at 600 rpm), batch 1, S0/X0, gave pre-separation HPLC phase ratio 0.169, aqueous target 0.800 and organic target 0.152. Its exact recipe repeat, batch 8, gave 0.178, 0.811 and 0.165. This repeat spread was much smaller than most material contrasts.

Holding S0 fixed, batches 1–4 changed X0→X3. Their organic target estimates were respectively 0.152, 0.315, 0.211 and 0.375; aqueous estimates were 0.800, 0.716, 0.784 and 0.615. Holding X0 fixed, batches 1, 5, 6 and 7 changed S0→S3 and gave organic estimates 0.152, 0.304, 0.229 and 0.338, with aqueous estimates 0.800, 0.702, 0.747 and 0.643. These differences generally exceed both the S0/X0 repeat spread and the declared channel-noise scale.

Phase-amount tests used S0/X0 and the baseline mixing. Batch 9 decreased added aqueous liquid to 0.020 L and increased extractant to 0.040 L: phase ratio rose to 0.394 and organic target to 0.355, while aqueous target fell to 0.627. Batch 10 used 0.055 L aqueous and 0.005 L extractant: phase ratio fell to 0.059, organic target to 0.067, and aqueous target rose to 0.944. Using the measured phase ratio to convert inventory fractions into an apparent organic/aqueous concentration ratio gives roughly 0.87 for batch 9, 0.93–0.94 for baseline batches 1 and 8, and 1.13 for batch 10. The low-volume endpoint amplifies measurement uncertainty, so this is approximate rather than evidence for an exact constant.

Mixing evidence was less decisive. Batch 11, mixed only 10 s at 100 rpm, gave organic target 0.152—identical to batch 1 within displayed precision and close to the repeat range. Batch 12, mixed 1200 s at 1000 rpm, gave 0.225, numerically above both baseline repeats. However, duration and speed changed together, neither condition was repeated, and batch 12 HPLC purity (0.932) was below the two baseline values (0.983 and 0.985).

The retention experiments established measurement semantics. After organic retention, final assays generally had phase ratio near 1 and negligible aqueous target; for example, batch 9 returned organic 0.339 and aqueous 0.000. After aqueous retention, assays generally had phase ratio near 0 and negligible organic target; batch 10 returned aqueous 0.998 and organic 0.006. Similar behavior occurred across the alternating retention choices. Small opposite-phase readings are compatible with instrumental/process noise and should not be interpreted as exact residual transfer.

Inference — A useful local account is that phase amount first controls how much capacity is available in each phase, while the selected S/X materials control the target’s relative affinity for those phases. Over the S0/X0 volume series, a roughly equilibrium-like concentration preference near unity explains why increasing organic phase volume strongly increases organic inventory without requiring an equally large change in intrinsic affinity. Both S and X materially affect this preference. X3 and X1 favored organic inventory more than X0 in the tested S0 background; S3 and S1 did likewise relative to S0 in the tested X0 background. This is evidence for material effects, but not yet a complete pairing law.

The baseline repeat supports reproducibility of the principal S0/X0 result. The phase-volume direction is also internally consistent and much larger than the repeat spread. By contrast, the study does not demonstrate that weak mixing limits extraction: its result overlapped baseline. The long/fast condition may have increased transfer, but it may instead have changed another process attribute, as suggested by the lower purity.

Conjecture and competing explanations — One conjecture is that mixing mainly affects the rate of approach to a material-specific partition equilibrium, with baseline and weak mixing already close enough to the same inventory split and long/fast mixing accessing a somewhat different state. Competing explanations are a speed-specific rather than duration-specific effect, mixing-induced impurity or transformation, systematic phase-volume estimation differences, or ordinary batch/instrument variation. Those alternatives cannot be separated because speed and duration were confounded and the extreme mixing conditions lacked repeats.

Scope and uncertainty — The material screen was a star centered on S0/X0, not a full S×X factorial. It therefore shows separate local effects of changing S or X but cannot establish additivity, interaction terms, or rank untested cross-pairings such as S3/X3. The approximate concentration-ratio account is supported only across three S0/X0 phase allocations at one total nominal liquid amount and one baseline mixing condition; it may fail at extreme ratios, different totals, multiple extraction stages, or other material pairs. The added solvent also contributes to the actual liquid system, so added aqueous and extractant volumes alone are not complete physical phase volumes. Finally, the two product channels do not always sum exactly to one, consistent with independent noisy estimates and possible process losses; closure deviations and missing channels were not treated as zero.

payload.rationale: I treated the phase fractions as complementary inventories governed locally by organic phase share and a material-dependent concentration preference. The S0/X0 volume series anchored the volume response; X3 increased organic affinity relative to X0, while S2 had a smaller positive effect. Strong mixing was treated as near the observed long/fast regime, but duration and speed effects remain confounded. Intervals widen for the untested S2/X3 pairing and mixing extrapolations, and represent uncertainty in noiseless fractions rather than future HPLC noise.

payload.report:
1. No instance-specific prior or material-property dossier was supplied; only anonymous material labels and instrument/operation contracts were provided. The least-tested self-developed law is the multiplicative, no-interaction extrapolation implicitly used for S2/X3 predictions. The campaign tested S effects only with X0 and X effects only with S0, so batches 1–7 do not establish behavior for crossed pairs. The assumed monotone mixing response is also weak: batch 11 overlapped the baseline repeats, while batch 12 changed duration and speed together and also had lower purity.

2. I would run S0/X0 at the common batch-1/8 phase amounts, but mix for 1200 s at 600 rpm. I would measure pre-separation HPLC target fractions, phase ratio, purity, and impurity signal. This single batch compares with batches 1/8 at the same speed but shorter duration, and with batch 12 at the same duration but higher speed. An organic fraction near batch 12 with baseline-like purity would favor duration-limited equilibration. A result near batches 1/8 would implicate high speed rather than duration. An increase accompanied by the purity loss seen in batch 12 would favor mixing-induced process change or target transformation over simple partition equilibration.

3. The final assays were underused quantitatively. Organic-retained assays in batches 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11 broadly tracked their pre-separation organic inventories, offering an independent check on phase assignment and transfer. Purity, impurity, recovery, and inventory closure were also underused; notably, batch 12’s lower purity weakens a pure-equilibration interpretation. Using noisy measured phase ratios to derive concentration preferences, especially in batch 10’s very small organic phase, may also have amplified error.

The least reliable predictions are Q08, Q11, and Q12 because S2/X3 was never tested; Q11 and Q12 additionally extrapolate unresolved speed effects. Q09 and Q10 are also uncertain because duration was never isolated experimentally. There is a real tension—not hindsight revision—between the sealed report’s statement that untested cross-pairings could not be ranked and the forced predictions’ multiplicative ranking of S2/X3. Likewise, the predictions imposed a monotone mixing trend despite the report calling mixing unresolved. Their wide, overlapping intervals partially represented those conjectures. Finally, every predicted aqueous/organic pair was forced to sum to one, whereas the report allowed possible target loss or transformation when discussing imperfect closure and purity; that conservation assumption was convenient but not conclusively established.
